# New Applications of 3SUM-Counting in Fine-Grained Complexity and Pattern Matching

**Authors:** Nick Fischer ††thanks: INSAIT, Sofia University “St. Kliment Ohridski”. nick.fischer@insait.ai. Partially funded by the Ministry of Education and Science of Bulgaria’s support for INSAIT, Sofia University “St. Kliment Ohridski” as part of the Bulgarian National Roadmap for Research Infrastructure. Parts of this work were done while the author was at Weizmann Institute of Science. Ce Jin ††thanks: Massachusetts Institute of Technology. cejin@mit.edu. Supported by NSF grants CCF-2129139 and CCF-2127597, and a Simons Investigator Award. Yinzhan Xu ††thanks: Massachusetts Institute of Technology. xyzhan@mit.edu. Supported by NSF Grant CCF-2330048, a Simons Investigator Award and HDR TRIPODS Phase II grant 2217058.

## Abstract

The 3SUM problem is one of the cornerstones of fine-grained complexity. Its study has led to countless lower bounds, but as has been sporadically observed before—and as we will demonstrate again—insights on 3SUM can also lead to algorithmic applications.

The starting point of our work is that we spend a lot of technical effort to develop new algorithms for 3SUM-type problems such as approximate 3SUM-counting, small-doubling 3SUM-counting, and a deterministic subquadratic-time algorithm for the celebrated Balog-Szemerédi-Gowers theorem from additive combinatorics. All of these are relevant in their own right and may prove useful for future research on 3SUM.

But perhaps even more excitingly, as consequences of these tools, we derive diverse new results in fine-grained complexity and pattern matching algorithms, answering open questions from many unrelated research areas. Specifically:

A recent line of research on the “short cycle removal” technique culminated in tight 3SUM-based lower bounds for various graph problems via randomized fine-grained reductions [Abboud, Bringmann, Fischer; STOC ’23] [Jin, Xu; STOC ’23]. In this paper we derandomize the reduction to the important 4-Cycle Listing problem, answering a main open question of [Fischer, Kaliciak, Polak; ITCS ’24].

We establish that #3SUM and 3SUM are fine-grained equivalent under deterministic reductions, derandomizing a main result of [Chan, Vassilevska Williams, Xu; STOC ’23].

We give a deterministic algorithm for the $(1+\epsilon)$ -approximate Text-to-Pattern Hamming Distances problem in time $n^{1+o(1)}\cdot\epsilon^{-1}$ . While there is a large body of work addressing the randomized complexity, this is the first deterministic improvement over Karloff’s $\widetilde{O}(n\epsilon^{-2})$ -time algorithm in over 30 years.

In the $k$ -Mismatch Constellation problem the input consists of two integer sets $A,B\subseteq[N]$ , and the goal is to test whether there is a shift $c$ such that $|(c+B)\setminus A|\leq k$ (i.e., whether $B$ shifted by $c$ matches $A$ up to $k$ mismatches). For moderately small $k$ the previously best running time was $\widetilde{O}(|A|\cdot k)$ [Cardoze, Schulman; FOCS ’98] [Fischer; SODA ’24]. We give a faster $|A|\cdot k^{2/3}\cdot N^{o(1)}$ -time algorithm in the regime where $|B|=\Theta(|A|)$ . This result also has implications for the $k$ -Mismatch String Matching with Wildcards problem.

## 1 Introduction

The famous 3SUM problem is to test whether a given set $A$ of $n$ integers contains a solution to the equation $a+b=c$ . It was hypothesized long ago that the naive $O(n^{2})$ -time algorithm for 3SUM is essentially best-possible [GO95], and this hypothesis has since evolved into a corner stone of fine-grained complexity theory, forming the basis of countless conditional lower bounds. In a recent result, Chan, Jin, Vassilevska Williams, and Xu [CJVX23] showcased that, quite surprisingly, some of the carefully crafted lower bound techniques can be turned into algorithms for seemingly unrelated problems, such as pattern matching on strings.

In this work we explore this paradigm further. We develop a colorful palette of new tools tailored towards 3SUM-type questions, often with a particular focus on deterministic algorithms, and often aided by tools from additive combinatorics such as the celebrated Balog-Szemerédi-Gowers (BSG) theorem. Then we apply these tools to derive various new fine-grained lower bounds—but also to design new and faster algorithms for pattern matching problems. We start with an exposition of our applications.

### 1.1 Application 1: Deterministic 3SUM-hardness

Recently, there has been an emerging interest in derandomizing fine-grained reductions from the 3SUM problem [CH20, CX24, FKP24]. This line of research follows two conceptual goals: (1) understanding the power of randomization in fine-grained complexity, and (2) establishing lower bounds that endure even if there turns out to be a truly subquadratic randomized algorithm for 3SUM. Formally, the goal is to establish conditional lower bound under the following deterministic hypothesis:

#### Hypothesis 1 (Deterministic 3SUM Hypothesis).

For any $\epsilon>0$ , there is no deterministic algorithm that solves 3SUM on $n$ numbers in $O(n^{2-\epsilon})$ time.

This is a weaker hypothesis than the usual 3SUM hypothesis, which commonly also allows randomized algorithms. See [FKP24] for a detailed discussion on the motivations of studying deterministic reductions from 3SUM.

Historically, the first result for derandomizing reductions from 3SUM is due to Chan and He [CH20], who derandomized the reduction from 3SUM to 3SUM Convolution. Said reduction, originally due to Pătraşcu [Păt10], plays a key role in complexity as it first related 3SUM to a non-geometric problem. Recently, Chan and Xu [CX24] showed a deterministic reduction from 3SUM to the All-Edges Sparse Triangle problem11 1 Given an $m$ -edge graph, determine whether each edge in the graph is in a triangle., whose randomized version was again shown in [Păt10].22 2 Technically, the reduction in [CX24] is from Exact Triangle to All-Edges Sparse Triangle (derandomizing an earlier reduction from [VX20]). Combined with prior work [CH20, VW13] this entails the claimed deterministic reduction from 3SUM to All-Edges Sparse Triangle. Independent to [CX24], Fischer, Kaliciak, and Polak [FKP24] studied deterministic reductions from 3SUM in a more systematic way. They derandomized the majority of formerly randomized reductions from 3SUM, including the reduction from 3SUM to All-Edges Sparse Triangle, $3$ -Linear Degeneracy Testing, Local Alignment and many more. This leads to an almost-complete derandomization, with the notable exception of the hardness results from three recent papers [ABKZ22, ABF23, JX23].

These three works [ABKZ22, ABF23, JX23] establish strong lower bounds for important graphs problems such as 4-Cycle Listing and Distance Oracles. They commonly rely on the “short cycle removal” technique, a technique that was first proposed by Abboud, Bringmann, Khoury and Zamir [ABKZ22] and independently optimized in [ABF23, JX23]. It is based on a structure-versus-randomness paradigm, on graphs or on numbers, which seems inherently randomized. Specifically, the key step in the refined proof [ABF23, JX23] is to reduce 3SUM to 3SUM instances with small additive energy33 3 The additive energy $\mathsf{E}(A)$ of an integer set $A$ is the number of tuples $(a,b,c,d)\in A^{4}$ with $a+b=c+d$ . . This key step utilizes the popular BSG theorem from additive combinatorics, and obtaining a deterministic algorithm for the BSG theorem is the main technical challenge for desired derandomization [FKP24]. Jin and Xu [JX23] additionally showed 3SUM-hardness for 4-Linear Degeneracy Testing, which also remained underandomized.

In this paper we derandomize the key step in [ABF23, JX23] and successfully design a deterministic reduction from general 3SUM instances to 3SUM instances with small additive energy:

#### Theorem 1.1.

For any constant $\delta>0$ , there is a deterministic fine-grained reduction from 3SUM to 3SUM with additive energy at most $n^{2+\delta}$ .

Naturally one of the main ingredients of the above theorem is a deterministic subquadratic-time algorithm for the constructive BSG theorem, which may be of independent interest (see Section 1.3).

With some more work, Theorem 1.1 implies the following lower bound for the 4-Cycle Listing problem (where the goal is to list all $4$ -cycles in a given undirected graph), resolving a main open question left by [FKP24].

#### Theorem 1.2.

Under the deterministic 3SUM hypothesis, there is no deterministic algorithm for 4-Cycle Listing on $n$ -node $m$ -edge graphs in $O(n^{2-\delta}+t)$ time or $O(m^{4/3-\delta}+t)$ time for any $\delta>0$ , where $t$ is the number of $4$ -cycles in the graph.

These lower bounds tightly match the upper bounds for 4-Cycle Listing [JX23, AKLS23].

We remark that the additional work needed to derive Theorem 1.2 from Theorem 1.1 does not easily follow from previous work, and is in fact somewhat technically involved. In [ABF23, JX23], the way to derive a randomized version of Theorem 1.2 from a randomized version of Theorem 1.1 is to first reduce low-energy 3SUM to All-Edges Sparse Triangle with few $4$ -cycles (morally, this is a “low-energy” variant of triangle detection in graphs). These reductions in [ABF23, JX23] are both randomized. Even though deterministic reductions from 3SUM to All-Edges Sparse Triangle are known [CX24, FKP24], they do not seem to preserve low energies. Our alternative reduction looks more like a direct derandomization of [ABF23], which makes the reduction more technically heavy. For instance, as a key technical tool it relies on derandomized version of the almost-additive hash functions used in [ABF23, JX23].

Utilizing our deterministic subquadratic-time algorithm for the constructive BSG theorem (which was a main ingredient in Theorem 1.1) we also show a deterministic fine-grained equivalence between 3SUM and #3SUM—the problem of counting the number of 3SUM solutions. This equivalence was first shown by Chan, Vassilevska Williams and Xu [CVX23] (by means of randomized reductions). As a technical bonus, and in contrast to [CVX23], our new reduction avoids the use of fast matrix multiplication (it relies on FFT instead).

#### Theorem 1.3.

#3SUM and 3SUM are subquadratically equivalent, under deterministic reductions.

### 1.2 Application 2: Pattern matching algorithms

Inspired by the previously observed connection [CJVX23] between tools in the fine-grained complexity of 3SUM on the one hand, and the design of pattern matching algorithms on the other hand, we have investigated how our toolset can further be algorithmically exploited. We offer two algorithms for natural pattern matching tasks.

#### Problem 1: Text-to-Pattern Hamming Distances.

In the Text-to-Pattern Hamming Distances problem (also known as Sliding Window Hamming Distances), we are given a pattern string $P$ of length $m$ and a text $T$ of length $n$ over some common alphabet $\Sigma$ , and the goal is to compute the Hamming distance (i.e., the number of mismatches) between $P$ and $T[i\mathinner{.\,.}i+m-1]$ for every shift $i\in[n-m]$ . This fundamental text-processing problem has been extensively studied in various settings [FP74, Abr87, Kar93, FG13, AGW13, KP15, KP18, CGK+20].

Of particular interest is approximate setting, where the typical goal is to compute $(1+\epsilon)$ -approximations of the Hamming distances. The history of this problem is rich, starting with a classical algorithm due to Karloff [Kar93] running in time $\widetilde{O}(n\epsilon^{-2})$ . At the time this was believed to be best-possible (in light of certain $\Omega(\epsilon^{-2})$ communication lower bounds [Woo04, JKS08]), and it was surprising when Kopelowitz and Porat [KP15] came up with an algorithm in time $\widetilde{O}(n\epsilon^{-1})$ ; see also [KP18] for a more streamlined algorithm. Then, in a very recent breakthrough, Chan, Jin, Vassilevska Williams, and Xu [CJVX23] gave an algorithm in $\widetilde{O}(n/\epsilon^{0.93})$ time, improving the dependence on $\epsilon^{-1}$ to sublinear. However, all of these algorithms are randomized.

Karloff [Kar93] also designed a deterministic algorithm running in time $O(n\epsilon^{-2}\log^{3}m)$ . In stark contrast to the progress by randomized algorithms, however, Karloff’s deterministic algorithm from more than 30 years ago has remained the state of the art. In our work we finally improve this $\epsilon^{-2}$ factor to $\epsilon^{-1}$ (albeit at the cost of incurring an extra $m^{o(1)}$ factor):

#### Theorem 1.4.

There is a deterministic algorithm solving $(1+\epsilon)$ -approximate Text-to-Pattern Hamming Distances in $nm^{o(1)}/\epsilon$ time.

This answers an open question explicitly asked by Kociumaka in a video talk on [CGK+20]44 4 https://youtu.be/WEiQjjTBX-4?t=2820 and by [CJVX23].

#### Problem 2: $k$ -Mismatch Constellation.

The Constellation problem is a natural geometric pattern matching task: Given two sets $A,B\subseteq\mathbb{Z}^{d}$ of at most $n$ points, the goal is to find all shifts $c\in\mathbb{Z}^{d}$ satisfying that $B+c\subseteq A$ . Intuitively, this models the task of identifying a certain constellation of stars $B$ in the night sky $A$ . But what if the constellation contains some mistakes? In the generalized $k$ -Mismatch Constellation problem the goal is to report all shifts $c$ with $|(c+B)\setminus A|\leq k$ (i.e., all occurrences that match the constellation in the night sky up to $k$ mismatches). It is known that we can assume all input points are in $\mathbb{Z}$ instead of $\mathbb{Z}^{d}$ without loss of generality [CS98, Fis24].

The study of this problem was initiated by Cardoze and Schulman [CS98]. Assuming the natural technical condition $k\leq(1-\eta)|B|$ for any fixed constant $\eta>0$ (which implies the output size is at most $n/\eta$ ), they designed a randomized algorithm in time $\widetilde{O}(nk)$ . Recently, Fischer [Fis24] revisited this problem and gave a deterministic $\widetilde{O}(nk)\cdot\operatorname{\mathrm{poly}}\log(N)$ time algorithm. Both of these results left open whether it is possible to achieve better algorithms, in time $O(nk^{1-\epsilon})$ , say, or perhaps even in near-linear time $\widetilde{O}(n)$ .

In fact, a side result by Chan, Vassilevska Williams, and Xu [CVX23, Lemma 8.4] implies an $n^{2-\Omega(1)}$ -time algorithm for this problem, which beats time $\widetilde{O}(nk)$ whenever $k$ is very large in terms of $n$ . As our second algorithmic contribution we significantly widen the range of $k$ for which we can improve upon the time $\widetilde{O}(nk)$ :

#### Theorem 1.5.

Let $A,B\subseteq[N]$ and let $1\leq k\leq 0.3|B|$ . There is a deterministic algorithm that solves $k$ -Mismatch Constellation in $|A|\cdot k^{2/3}\cdot(|A|/|B|)^{2/3}\cdot N^{o(1)}$ time. If randomization is allowed, then the $N^{o(1)}$ factor can be replaced by $\operatorname{\mathrm{poly}}\log(N)$ .

Notably, this algorithm runs in time $nk^{2/3}N^{o(1)}$ in the regime where $|B|=\Theta(|A|)$ (and $k$ is arbitrary). We improve upon the $\widetilde{O}(nk)$ baseline in the broader range $|B|\gg|A|/\sqrt{k}$ . (Counterintuitively, this problem indeed becomes harder the smaller $B$ is as then there could be completely separate structured regions in $A$ in which $B$ could be approximately matched.)

But can we do even better? In particular, there is no evidence that the problem cannot even be solved in near-linear time $\widetilde{O}(n)$ , irrespective of $k$ . Relatedly, in the $k$ -Bounded Text-to-Pattern Hamming Distances problem (where all distances exceeding $k$ can be reported as $\infty$ in Text-to-Pattern Hamming Distances), an algorithm in time $\widetilde{O}(n+k\sqrt{n})$ is known [GU18], in the setting where the text and pattern both have length $\Theta(n)$ . This running time becomes near-linear when $k$ is small ( $k\leq n^{\epsilon}$ , say). These two problems appear similar in nature in that for both problems the task is about shifts that result in at most $k$ mismatches. So can we achieve a similar result for $k$ -Mismatch Constellation?

Perhaps surprisingly, we prove that this is not possible—at least not by combinatorial55 5 In the context of fine-grained complexity and algorithm design, we informally say that an algorithm is combinatorial if it does not rely on algebraic fast matrix multiplication. It has emerged as a powerful paradigm to prove lower bounds for combinatorial based on the BMM hypothesis stating that there is no combinatorial algorithm for Boolean matrix multiplication in time $O(n^{3-\epsilon})$ (for all $\epsilon>0$ ). See e.g. [AV14, Wil18, GU18] and the references therein. algorithms:

#### Theorem 1.6.

Under the BMM hypothesis, combinatorial algorithms solving $k$ -Mismatch Constellation requires $\sqrt{k}n^{1-o(1)}$ time for sets of size $\Theta(n)$ .

This lower bound leaves a gap of $k^{1/6}$ to our algorithm. We leave it as an open question to close this gap, and to make further progress on the setting where $|B|\ll|A|$ .

#### Problem 3: $k$ -Mismatch String Matching with Wildcards.

Interestingly, our algorithm for $k$ -Mismatch Constellation also implies a new algorithm for the following well-studied problem [CEPR09, CEPR10, CP10, NR17, BCS24]: given a text string $T\in\Sigma^{n}$ , a pattern string $P\in(\Sigma\cup\{\diamondsuit\})^{m}$ , and integer $1\leq k\leq m$ , find all occurrences of $P$ inside $T$ allowing up to $k$ Hamming mismatches, where the wildcard $\diamondsuit\notin\Sigma$ can match any single character. Note that the wildcards appear only in the pattern and not in the text.

By a simple reduction from this problem to the $k$ -Mismatch Constellation problem, we obtain the following result as an immediate corollary of Theorem 1.5:

#### Corollary 1.7.

There is a deterministic algorithm that solves $k$ -Mismatch String Matching with Wildcards (in the pattern only) in time $k^{2/3}n^{1+o(1)}$ . If randomization is allowed, then the $n^{o(1)}$ factor can be replaced by $\operatorname{\mathrm{poly}}\log(n)$ .

The proof of this corollary from Theorem 1.5 is short and straightforward (see Section 11.4). Moreover, we can get a faster algorithm by adjusting parameters and simplifying a few steps in the proof of Theorem 1.5:

#### Theorem 1.8.

There is a deterministic algorithm that solves $k$ -Mismatch String Matching with Wildcards (in the pattern only) in time $k^{1/2}n^{1+o(1)}$ . If randomization is allowed, then the $n^{o(1)}$ factor can be replaced by $\operatorname{\mathrm{poly}}\log(n)$ .

We now briefly compare Theorem 1.8 with previous algorithms for $k$ -Mismatch String Matching with Wildcards (see [BCS24] for a more comprehensive overview). When wildcards are allowed in both the text and the pattern, [CEPR09, CEPR10] gave an algorithm in $\widetilde{O}(\min\{nk,n\sqrt{m}\})$ time. When wildcards are allowed either in the text only or in the pattern only, [CP10] gave an algorithm in $\widetilde{O}(n(mk)^{1/3})$ time. Our Theorem 1.8 is faster than these algorithms but only applies when all wildcards are in the pattern. More recent works [NR17, BCS24] gave fast algorithms parameterized by the number of wildcards and/or the number of contiguous segments of wildcards in the input.

### 1.3 Technical tools and overview

In this section, we list some of our new technical tools for proving the aforementioned results and also discuss some intuition for proving some of the results.

#### Tool I: Approximate 3SUM counting.

The first tool is an efficient deterministic algorithm for approximate 3SUM counting: Given integer (multi-)sets $A$ and $B$ , it approximately counts the number of times each number $c$ can be represented as a sum $a+b$ for $a\in A$ and $b\in B$ .

Formally, we write $1_{A}$ to denote the indicator vector of a (multi-)set $A$ , and use $\star$ between two vectors to denote their convolution (see formal definitions in Section 2). In particular, $1_{A}\star 1_{B}$ denotes a vector whose $c$ -th coordinate is the number of choices for picking $(a,b)\in A\times B$ so that $a+b=c$ .

#### Theorem 1.9 (Deterministic Popular Sums Approximation).

Let $A,B\subseteq[N]$ be multisets of size at most $N$ and let $\epsilon>0$ . There is a deterministic algorithm that runs in time $(\epsilon^{-1}|A|+|B|)\cdot N^{o(1)}$ and computes a vector $f$ of sparsity $\lVert f\rVert_{0}\leq O(\epsilon^{-1}|A|\log^{2}N)$ , such that $\lVert f-(1_{A}\star 1_{B})\rVert_{\infty}\leq\epsilon|B|$ .

To the best of our knowledge, this lemma has not explicitly appeared in the literature (even with randomization allowed). A randomized version of Theorem 1.9 is simple,66 6 We can randomly pick a prime $p=\Theta(\epsilon^{-1}|A|\log N)$ , and then compute $\sum_{i\equiv s\pmod{p}}(1_{A}\star 1_{B})[i]$ for every $s\in\mathbb{F}_{p}$ using FFT in $O(p\log p)=\widetilde{O}(\epsilon^{-1}|A|)$ time. For every index $i$ , the expected value of $\sum_{i^{\prime}\equiv i\pmod{p},i\neq i^{\prime}}(1_{A}\star 1_{B})[i^{\prime}]$ can be bounded by $O(\frac{|A||B|}{p/\log N})=O(\epsilon|B|)$ . Thus, by repeating $O(\log N)$ times, there must be one iteration where the mod $p$ bucket of $i$ is an additive $O(\epsilon|B|)$ approximation of $i$ , with high probability (we also have to recover the index of $i$ given its bucket, which can be achieved, say, by random sampling) but the deterministic version needs more care.

Theorem 1.9 is used as a subroutine in almost every result in this paper. For example, one useful application is to estimate the number of 4SUM solutions (which can be used for estimating the additive energy of a set) on inputs $A,B,C,D$ . To do this, we simply approximate $1_{A}\star 1_{B}$ by $f$ and approximate $1_{C}\star 1_{D}$ by $g$ using Theorem 1.9, and sum up $\sum_{x}f[x]g[-x]$ . Theorem 1.9 is also used in the proof of our deterministic BSG theorem (to be described later).

As another important application, combining Theorem 1.9 with the previous techniques due to Gawrychowski and Uznański [GU18] also implies our deterministic Text-to-Pattern Hamming Distances algorithm (Theorem 1.4). For the details, we refer to Section 8. But to illustrate the intuition behind the connection to Theorem 1.9, we will describe a very simple $\epsilon^{-1}n^{1+o(1)}$ time algorithm computing an additive $\epsilon m$ -approximation here.

For each symbol $s\in\Sigma$ , let $A_{s}:=\{j:T[j]=s\}$ and $B_{s}:=\{k:P[k]=s\}$ . Then the Hamming distance between $T[i+1\mathinner{.\,.\allowbreak}i+m]$ and $P[1\mathinner{.\,.\allowbreak}m]$ can be expressed as

$$ |P|-\sum_{s\in\Sigma}(1_{A_{s}}\star 1_{-B_{s}})[i]. $$

For each $s\in\Sigma$ , we can use Theorem 1.9 to compute in $(\epsilon^{-1}|A_{s}|+|B_{s}|)\cdot n^{o(1)}$ time a sparse vector $f_{s}$ satisfying that $\|f_{s}-1_{A_{s}}\star 1_{-B_{s}}\|_{\infty}\leq\epsilon|B_{s}|$ . Thus, for each index $i$ we can approximate the Hamming distance by $|P|-\sum_{s\in\Sigma}f_{s}[i]$ with an additive error of at most

$$ \sum_{s\in\Sigma}\big\lvert\big(f_{s}-1_{A_{s}}\star 1_{-B_{s}}\big)[i]\big\rvert\leq\sum_{s\in\Sigma}\epsilon|B_{s}|=\epsilon m. $$

The total time complexity is $\sum_{s\in\Sigma}(\epsilon^{-1}|A_{s}|+|B_{s}|)\cdot n^{o(1)}=\epsilon^{-1}n^{1+o(1)}$ .

#### Tool II: Small-doubling 3SUM counting.

The next technical tool is also for 3SUM counting, but in a different setting. This time we insist on exact counts, but we assume that the input is additively structured. Specifically, recall the definition of the sumset $A+A=\{a+b:a,b\in A\}$ . The doubling constant of a set is defined as the ratio $K=\frac{|A+A|}{|A|}$ . Intuitively, highly additively-structured sets (such as intervals or arithmetic progressions) have small doubling constant, whereas unstructured sets (such as random sets) have large doubling constant. The following theorem states that we can solve 3SUM counting exactly, provided that at least one input set has sufficiently small doubling constant:

#### Theorem 1.10 (Deterministic small-doubling 3SUM-counting; simplified from Theorem 4.1).

Given sets $A,B,C\subseteq[N]$ , where $|A+A|=K|A|$ , we can deterministically compute $(1_{C}\star 1_{-B})[a]$ for all $a\in A$ in time complexity $O\big(K\sqrt{|A||B||C|}\cdot N^{o(1)}\big)$ .

In particular, when $|A|,|B|,|C|\leq n$ , the time complexity becomes $O(Kn^{1.5}N^{o(1)})$ , which for small $K$ improves upon the standard quadratic-time algorithm for 3SUM. Previously, Jin and Xu [JX23] showed a randomized 3SUM algorithm in this regime in $O(Kn^{1.5}\operatorname{\mathrm{poly}}\log N)$ time (and Abboud, Bringmann, and Fischer [ABF23] also independently showed a randomized algorithm in $\operatorname{\mathrm{poly}}(K)n^{2-\Omega(1)}$ time). Our Theorem 4.1 simultaneously (i) derandomizes these results, (ii) extends them to the counting version of 3SUM, and (iii) also allow $A,B,C$ to differ in size. The latter two new features turn out to be crucial for our $k$ -Mismatch Constellation algorithm.

The randomized version of this small-doubling 3SUM algorithm is a key step in the randomized fine-grained reductions in [ABF23, JX23] from 3SUM to small-energy 3SUM (and thus a stepping stone in the chain of reductions to 4-Cycle Listing and Approximate Distance Oracles). Small doubling instances for $k$ -SUM and integer programming have also been studied by Randolph in his thesis [Ran24].

#### Tool III: Almost-additive hashing with small seed length.

A family of hash functions $h$ is called additive if it satisfies $h(x+y)=h(x)+h(y)$ , and almost-additive if $h(x+y)-h(x)-h(y)$ takes only constantly many different values. (Almost-)additive hashing has been playing an important role for 3SUM for a long time [BDP08, Păt10], and also the modern fine-grained reductions oftentimes rely on such hash functions. The most common use cases is to reduce the universe size in the 3SUM problem (typically at the cost of introducing some few false solutions). In [FKP24] it was shown that this application can be derandomized building on the family of hash functions $h(x)=x\;\,({\bmod}\>p)$ (where $p$ is a random prime).

Unfortunately, for our purposes this derandomization result is often not sufficient. The reason is technical: For some applications, specifically the reductions based on arithmetic short cycle removal [ABF23, JX23], we additionally need the hash function to be 3-wise independent. While it is provably impossible for a hash family to be (almost-)linear and 3-wise independent at the same time, this can at least approximately be achieved (see Section 5). To derandomize this more constrained hash family, we come up with a creative construction that besides the hash function $h(x)=x\;\,({\bmod}\>p)$ from before, also throws derandomization by $\epsilon$ -biased sets [AGHP92] into the mix.

#### Tool IV: Deterministic BSG theorem.

Putting together the previous three tools, we manage show a deterministic subquadratic-time algorithm to compute the Balog-Szemerédi-Gowers (BSG) theorem:

#### Theorem 1.11 (Deterministic subquadratic-time BSG theorem; simplified from Theorem 6.1).

Given set $A\subseteq[N]$ and $K\geq 1$ such that the additive energy is $\mathsf{E}(A)\geq|A|^{3}/K$ , we can deterministically find a subset $A^{\prime}\subseteq A$ in $(|A|^{2}/K^{2}+K^{13}|A|)N^{o(1)}$ time, such that $|A^{\prime}|\geq|A|/(64K)$ and $|A^{\prime}+A^{\prime}|\leq K^{16}|A|\cdot N^{o(1)}$ .

In words, the BSG theorem [BS94, Gow01] states that a set with high additive energy must contain a large subset of small doubling. The constructive BSG theorem was first used by Chan and Lewenstein [CL15], and later played a crucial role in the randomized fine-grained reductions of [ABF23, JX23], and different versions of BSG theorem were proved in [CVX23]. All previous proofs for (versions of) the constructive BSG theorem were randomized, except the one in [CL15]: they showed a deterministic algorithm that runs in $O(n^{\omega})$ time for constant values of $K$ , where $\omega<2.372$ [DWZ23, VXXZ24] is the matrix multiplication exponent. But this running time is not efficient enough for our purposes; we really need subquadratic time. All other previous proofs for constructive BSG theorem use randomness crucially. One (less crucial) use of randomness was for approximating the degree of nodes in certain bipartite graphs defined by the additive relation of the input sets; for this part, the degrees actually correspond to 3SUM solution counts, and hence can be derandomized using our Theorem 1.9. However, a more crucial use of randomness in the previous proof is due to the probabilistic method, specifically the method of dependent random choice. For this part, a naive derandomization would require enumerating all possibilities, taking (at least) quadratic time.

Although our deterministic constructive BSG is slower than known randomized versions (which run in $\widetilde{O}(|A|\operatorname{\mathrm{poly}}(K))$ time [CL15, ABF23, JX23]), and provide worse quantitative bounds, it still runs in subquadratic time when $K$ is not too small.

Roughly speaking, the proof of our deterministic BSG theorem uses the following strategy: We do not know how to overcome the aforementioned quadratic barrier for derandomizing the probabilistic method, but we can afford to run this slow derandomization on some much smaller subset $A_{0}\subseteq A$ . Then, we will use the results computed on this small subset $A_{0}$ to extract the desired small-doubling large subset $A^{\prime}\subseteq A$ . Naturally, if $A_{0}$ is chosen smaller, then this derandomization is faster, at the cost of worsening the doubling constant of the extracted subset $A^{\prime}$ . In order to make such extraction possible, we need to make subset $A_{0}\subseteq A$ inherit the high additive energy of $A$ (roughly speaking, if $\mathsf{E}(A)\geq|A|^{3}/K$ , then we would like $\mathsf{E}(A_{0})\geq|A_{0}|^{3-o(1)}/K$ ). Simply uniformly subsampling $A_{0}\subseteq A$ would cause too much loss, and we need to do something more technical: we (deterministically) pick a certain almost-additive hash function (see Section 5), mapping $A$ to roughly $|A|/|A_{0}|$ buckets, and then pick one of the buckets as our $A_{0}$ . This is exactly where our tool III, the deterministic almost-additive hash functions, come into play. We find it interesting that these hash families find an application here that is completely different from their original intent [ABF23, JX23].

#### Tool V: 3SUM counting for popular sums.

The fifth and final tool we introduce is yet another variant of 3SUM counting: This time the goal is to exactly count 3SUM solutions, but only those involving the most popular elements (i.e., those elements $s$ that are contained in many 3-sums):

#### Theorem 1.12 (Deterministic 3SUM-counting for popular sums).

Given sets $A,B\subseteq[N]$ , $|A|,|B|\leq n$ , and a parameter $k\geq 1$ , there is a deterministic algorithm that returns $S=\{s:(1_{A}\star 1_{B})[s]\geq|A|/k\}$ and exactly computes $(1_{A}\star 1_{B})[s]$ for all $s\in S$ in $O(k^{2}|A|^{2-3/128}\cdot N^{o(1)})$ time.

Chan, Vassilevska Williams and Xu [CVX23, Lemma 8.4] gave a randomized subquadratic-time algorithm for this task using fast matrix multiplication. Our Theorem 1.12 derandomizes [CVX23, Lemma 8.4], and does not require fast matrix multiplication, but the running time has a worse exponent (but is still subquadratic).

In fact, establishing Theorem 1.12 immediately completes the proof of Theorem 1.3. Recall that this theorem was originally proven in [CVX23] (by means of randomized reductions), and tracing through their proofs it is easy to check that replacing their Lemma 8.4 by our Theorem 1.3 replaces the only randomized step by a deterministic alternative.

#### Techniques for the $k$ -Mismatch Constellation algorithm.

Throughout the overview we have encountered hints for the proofs of all our algorithmic applications, except for the algorithm for $k$ -Mismatch Constellation; let us finally provide some overview for this result. Similar to previous work of Fischer [Fis24], we solve $k$ -Mismatch Constellation by solving a Partial Convolution instance. That is, given sets $A,B,C\subseteq[N]$ , where $C$ is a set of candidate answers such that every $c\in C$ is promised to satisfy $|(c+B)\setminus A|\leq O(k)$ , and the goal is to exactly compute $|(c+B)\setminus A|$ for all $c\in C$ . The algorithm of Fischer [Fis24] (which can be viewed as a certain transposed version of sparse convolution) solves this task in $\widetilde{O}(|A|+|B+C|)\leq\widetilde{O}(|A|+k|C|)$ time, which is at most $\widetilde{O}(k|A|)$ since $|C|=O(|A|)$ . Our algorithm uses a win-win argument: If $|C|$ is small, then Fischer’s algorithm is already faster than $\widetilde{O}(k|A|)$ . Otherwise, if $|C|$ is large, then we show that the input instance must have very rich additive structure. In particular, $C$ must have low doubling constant, and there is very large subset $B^{\prime}\subseteq B$ of size $|B^{\prime}|\geq|B|-O(k)$ such that the sumset $B^{\prime}+C$ is small. Then, we separately compute with the contribution of $B^{\prime}$ and $B\setminus B^{\prime}$ to the answers:

- • For $B^{\prime}$ , based on the small sumset size $|B^{\prime}+C|$ , we use the technique of Fischer [Fis24] to compute their contribution.

- • For $B\setminus B^{\prime}$ , we take advantage of the small doubling of $C$ , and use our small-doubling #3SUM algorithm (Theorem 1.10) to compute their contribution.

### 1.4 Discussions and open questions

Our work further explores the role of additive structure in the context of fine-grained complexity and pattern matching problems. We believe the various technical tools developed in this paper can find future applications.

We conclude with some natural open questions arising from our work.

- 1. Can we deterministically solve $(1+\epsilon)$ Text-to-Pattern Hamming Distances in time complexity $O((1/\epsilon)^{1-c}n^{1+o(1)})$ for some constant $c>0$ ? The recent breakthrough of [CJVX23] achieved such a running time using randomization. One of their key steps is to compute the multiplicities of popular sums up to very high precision, using the techniques from the randomized algorithm of [CVX23] that solves #3SUM for popular sums. This part can already be derandomized by our Theorem 1.12. However, another step in the proof of [CJVX23] involves analyzing the error of random subsampling by bounding the variance, and we do not know how to derandomize such arguments.

- 2. Our derandomized reduction from low-energy 3SUM problem to the 4-Cycle Listing problem turned out to be much more technical than its randomized counterpart in [ABF23, JX23]. Due to similar technical reasons, Theorem 1.1 does not immediately show conditional lower bound for Distance Oracles under the deterministic 3SUM hypothesis, and it seems harder to derandomize the reduction in [ABF23, JX23] to Distance Oracles because the reduction needs to bound the number of longer cycles, which seems more difficult to control. We leave it as an interesting open problem to derandomize the reduction from 3SUM to Distance Oracles.

- 3. Another underandomized result in [JX23] is the 3SUM hardness for 4-Linear Degeneracy Testing (whereas 3-Linear Degeneracy Testing has deterministic 3SUM hardness, as shown earlier in [DGS20]). We expect a larger barrier in derandomizing this reduction. The reason is that, in order to show hardness for 4-Linear Degeneracy Testing, [JX23] first showed hardness for 3SUM instances whose additive energy is $2n^{2}-n$ (i.e., Sidon sets). This suggests that one might need to first improve the bound of Theorem 1.1 from $O(n^{2+\delta})$ to $2n^{2}-n$ , which seems challenging using our current method. (In contrast, it is totally reasonable that Theorem 1.1 could be used in a black-box way, combined with additional ideas, to show lower bound for Distance Oracles under the deterministic 3SUM hypothesis.)

- 4. Our algorithm for $k$ -Mismatch Constellation only achieves improvement in the $|B|\approx|A|$ regime. Can we show faster algorithms when $|B|$ can be much smaller than $|A|$ ?

- 5. Can we relax Theorem 1.8 to allow wildcards in both the pattern and the text?

## 2 Preliminaries

Let $\mathbb{Z}$ and $\mathbb{N}=\mathbb{Z}_{\geq 0}$ denote the integers and the non-negative integers respectively. Let $[n]=\{0,1,\dots,n-1\}$ . We use $\widetilde{O}(f)$ to denote $O(f\cdot\operatorname{\mathrm{poly}}\log f)$ .

For two sets $A,B$ , define their sumset $A+B=\{a+b:a\in A,b\in B\}$ and difference set $A-B=\{a-b:a\in A,b\in B\}$ . Let $-A=\{-a:a\in A\}$ . We define the iterative sumset $kA$ by the recursive definition $kA=(k-1)A+A$ , and $1A=A$ .

For a vector $v$ , we use $v[i]$ to refer to its $i$ -th coordinate, and denote $\supp(v)=\{i:v[i]\neq 0\}$ , $\|v\|_{0}=|\supp(v)|$ , $\|v\|_{\infty}=\max_{i}|v[i]|$ , and $\|v\|_{1}=\sum_{i}|v[i]|$ . We say $v$ is $s$ -sparse if $\|v\|_{0}\leq s$ .

The convolution of two length- $N$ vectors $u,v$ is defined as the vector $u\star v$ of length $2N-1$ with

$$ (u\star v)[k]=\sum_{\begin{subarray}{c}i,j\in[N]\\
i+j=k\end{subarray}}u[i]\cdot v[j]. $$

The cyclic convolution $u\star_{m}v$ is the length- $m$ vector with

$$ (u\star_{m}v)[k]=\sum_{\begin{subarray}{c}i,j\in[N]\\
i+j\equiv k\,(\mathrm{mod}\,m)\end{subarray}}u[i]\cdot v[j]. $$

In this paper we often work with multisets, in which an element is allowed to occur multiple times. For a multiset $A\subseteq[N]$ ,77 7 By “multiset $A\subseteq[N]$ ” we mean each $a\in A$ is in $[N]$ but may have multiplicity greater than $1$ . let $1_{A}\in\mathbb{Z}_{\geq 0}^{N}$ be its indicator vector where $1_{A}[i]$ denotes the multiplicity of $i$ in $A$ . Following this notion, the size of the multiset $A$ is $|A|=\lVert 1_{A}\rVert_{1}$ , $(1_{A}\star 1_{B})[i]$ denotes the number of representations $i=a+b$ for $a\in A$ and $b\in B$ , and $(1_{A}\star_{m}1_{B})[i]$ denotes the number of representations $i\equiv a+b\;\,({\bmod}\>m)$ for $a\in A$ and $b\in B$ .

The additive energy between two sets $A,B\subset\mathbb{Z}$ is

$$ \displaystyle\mathsf{E}(A,B) \displaystyle=|\{(a,a^{\prime},b,b^{\prime})\in A\times A\times B\times B:a+b=a^{\prime}+b^{\prime}\}| \displaystyle=\sum_{s}(1_{A}\star 1_{-A})[s]\cdot(1_{B}\star 1_{-B})[s]=\sum_{s}((1_{A}\star 1_{B})[s])^{2}. $$

The additive energy of a set $A\subset\mathbb{Z}$ is $\mathsf{E}(A)=\mathsf{E}(A,A)$ . We have $\mathsf{E}(A)\mathsf{E}(B)\geq\mathsf{E}(A,B)^{2}$ by Cauchy-Schwarz inequality.

We need the deterministic nonnegative sparse convolution algorithm by Bringmann, Fischer, and Nakos [BFN22].

#### Lemma 2.1 (Sparse convolution [BFN22, Theorem 1]).

Given two nonnegative vectors $x,y\in\mathbb{N}^{N}$ , there is a deterministic algorithm that computes $x\star y$ in $O\big(\|x\star y\|_{0}\cdot\operatorname{\mathrm{poly}}\log(N\|x\|_{\infty}\|y\|_{\infty})\big)$ time.

We need the following partial convolution algorithm by Fischer [Fis24].

#### Lemma 2.2 (Partial convolution [Fis24, Theorem 4.1]).

Given sets $A,B,C\subseteq[N]$ , and $x,y\in\mathbb{Z}^{N}$ with $\supp(x)\subseteq A,\supp(y)\subseteq B$ , there is a deterministic algorithm that computes $(x\star y)[c]$ for all $c\in C$ in $O\big((|A|+|C-B|)\cdot\operatorname{\mathrm{poly}}\log(N\|x\|_{\infty}\|y\|_{\infty})\big)$ time.

## 3 Tool I: Deterministic Approximate 3SUM Counting

The goal of this section is to prove Theorem 1.9, restated below.

See 1.9

As an immediate corollary, this theorem implies the following result for 3SUM:

#### Corollary 3.1 (Approximate 3SUM Counting).

Let multisets $A,B\subseteq[N]$ , set $C\subseteq[N]$ , and let $\epsilon>0$ . There is a deterministic algorithm that runs in time $\widetilde{O}((\epsilon^{-1}|A|+|B|+|C|)\cdot N^{o(1)})$ and computes approximations $f(c)$ , for all $c\in C$ , such that

$$ |f(c)-(1_{A}\star 1_{B})[c]|\leq\epsilon|B|. $$

For the proof of Theorem 1.9, we rely on the following weaker lemma to compute approximations with bounded total error but unbounded coordinate-wise error:

#### Lemma 3.2.

Let $A,B\subseteq[N]$ be multisets, let $C\subseteq[N]$ be a set and let $\epsilon>0$ . There is a deterministic algorithm that runs in time $\widetilde{O}((\epsilon^{-1}|A|+|B|+|C|)\cdot N^{o(1)})$ and computes an approximation $g(c)$ for each $c\in C$ such that:

- • $g(c)\geq(1_{A}\star 1_{B})[c]$ , and

- • $\sum_{c\in C}g(c)-(1_{A}\star 1_{B})[c]\leq\min(\epsilon|B|\,|C|,|A|\,|B|\log N)$ .

#### Proof.

We follow the deterministic hashing procedure as by Chan and Lewenstein [CL15] and later applied in [CH20, FKP24]. The idea is to select a modulus $m\approx\epsilon^{-1}|A|+|C|$ as the product of several small primes. Our goal is to achieve two objectives: (1) We want to isolate a constant fraction of elements in $C$ modulo $m$ , and (2) we want to reduce the number of pseudo-solutions modulo $m$ (that is, triples $(a,b,c)\in A\times B\times C$ with $a+b\neq c$ and $a+b\equiv c\;\,({\bmod}\>m)$ ) to $\approx\epsilon|B|\,|C|$ . Then, for all isolated elements $c\in C$ we can approximate $(1_{A}\star 1_{B})[c]$ by the number of pseudo-solutions involving $c$ with total error $\approx\epsilon|B|\,|C|$ .

We now describe this algorithm in detail. Let $P$ be a parameter to be fixed later. Throughout we maintain a set $C^{*}\subseteq C$ which is initially $C^{*}\leftarrow C$ . We call a pair $(c^{*},c)\in C^{*}\times C$ a collision under $m$ if $c^{*}\neq c$ and $c^{*}\equiv c\;\,({\bmod}\>m)$ , and denote the number of collisions under $m$ by $\operatorname{coll}_{C^{*}}(m)$ . We say that $c^{*}$ is isolated under $m$ if there is no collision $(c^{*},c)$ under $m$ . Note that given any $m$ we can compute $\operatorname{coll}_{C^{*}}(m)$ in time $\widetilde{O}(|C|+m)$ . While $C^{*}\neq\emptyset$ , we repeat the following steps:

- 1. Initialize $m:=1$

- 2. Repeat the following steps $R:=\lceil\log(\epsilon^{-1}|A|\log N+2|C|)/\log P\rceil$ times: 2.1 Test all primes $p\in[10(P\log_{P}N)\log(P\log_{P}N),20(P\log_{P}N)\log(P\log_{P}N)]$ exhaustively and select one – such that $\operatorname{coll}_{C^{*}}(mp)\leq\frac{\operatorname{coll}_{C^{*}}(m)}{P}$ , and – such that $\#\{(a,b,c)\in A\times B\times C:a+b\equiv c\;\,({\bmod}\>mp)\}$ is minimized (note that this quantity can be computed by FFT in time $\widetilde{O}(mp)$ ) 2.2 Update $m:=m\cdot p$

- 3. Compute $g^{\prime}(c)=\#\{(a,b)\in A\times B:a+b\equiv c\;\,({\bmod}\>m)\}$ for all $c\in C$ by FFT in time $\widetilde{O}(m)$

- 4. Compute the subset of elements $c^{*}\in C^{*}$ that is isolated under $m$

- 5. For each isolated element $c^{*}\in C^{*}$ : 5.1. Set $g(c^{*}):=g^{\prime}(c^{*})$ 5.2. Remove $c^{*}$ from $C^{*}$

Correctness. As a first step we argue that (1) we can always select a prime in step 22.1 satisfying the two conditions, and (2) for the final modulus (obtained when step 2 ends) we have that

$$ S(m):=\#\{(a,b,c)\in A\times B\times C:a+b\neq c,a+b\equiv c\;\,({\bmod}\>m)\}\leq\frac{\epsilon}{\log N}\cdot|B|\,|C|. $$

By a crude quantitative version of the Prime Number Theorem, there are at least $4P\log_{P}N$ primes in the interval $[10(P\log_{P}N)\log(P\log_{P}N),20(P\log_{P}N)\log(P\log_{P}N)]$ (see e.g. [RS62, Corollary 3]). So focus on any inner iteration of step 22.1, and suppose that we select prime $p$ from this interval uniformly at random. For (1), for any fixed pair $(c_{0},c)$ ( $c_{0}\neq c$ ), since $c-c_{0}$ has at most $\log_{P}N$ prime factors larger than $P$ , we know $(c_{0},c)$ becomes a collision modulo $p$ with probability at most $\frac{\log_{P}N}{4P(\log_{P}N)}=\frac{1}{4P}$ . Thus, the expected number of collisions modulo $p$ among the $\operatorname{coll}(m)$ collisions modulo $m$ is at most $\frac{\operatorname{coll}(m)}{4P}$ , and by Markov’s bound the prime satisfies $\operatorname{coll}(mp)\leq\frac{\operatorname{coll}(m)}{P}$ with probability at least $\frac{3}{4}$ . For the final modulus $m$ , in particular we have that

$$ \operatorname{coll}(m)\leq\frac{|C^{*}|\,|C|}{P^{R}}\leq\frac{|C^{*}|\,|C|}{2|C|}\leq\frac{|C^{*}|}{2}. $$

For (2), one can similarly argue about the number of false positives. A random prime $p$ reduces the number of false positives modulo $mp$ in expectation by a factor $\frac{1}{4P}$ and thus by a factor $\frac{1}{P}$ with probability at least $\frac{3}{4}$ . By a union bound both events happen simultaneously with positive probability. In particular, we can pick the prime minimizing

$$ \#\{(a,b,c)\in A\times B\times C:a+b\equiv c\;\,({\bmod}\>mp)\}, $$

which equivalently minimizes

$$ \#\{(a,b,c)\in A\times B\times C:a+b\neq c,a+b\equiv c\;\,({\bmod}\>mp)\}, $$

to ultimately obtain that

$$ S(m)\leq\frac{|A|\,|B|\,|C|}{P^{R}}\leq\frac{|A|\,|B|\,|C|}{\epsilon^{-1}|A|\log N}=\frac{\epsilon}{\log N}\cdot|B|\,|C|. $$

Next, we analyze the number of iterations of the algorithm. From the bound on the number of collisions above we infer that at least half of the elements in $C^{*}$ are isolated. As in each iteration we remove all isolated elements from $C^{*}$ , it follows that the number of iterations is bounded by $\log|C|\leq\log N$ .

Finally, we analyze the approximations $g(c^{*})$ . Focus on any iteration of the algorithm. On the one hand, since we set $g(c^{*}):=g^{\prime}(c^{*})$ which equals the pseudo-solutions equal to $c^{*}$ , we must have that $g(c^{*})\geq(1_{A}\star 1_{B})[c^{*}]$ . On the other hand, note that each pseudo-solution contributes at most $1$ to the sum $\sum_{\text{$c^{*}\in C^{*}$ isolated}}g^{\prime}(c^{*})$ and hence the total contribution of the pseudo-solutions is at most $\frac{\epsilon}{\log N}\cdot|B|\,|C|$ . But as in each iteration we only assign the values $g(c^{*})$ for the isolated elements $c^{*}\in C^{*}$ and as the algorithm terminates after at most $\log N$ iterations, it follows that indeed

$$ \sum_{c\in C}g(c)-(1_{A}\star 1_{B})[c]\leq\epsilon|B|\,|C|. $$

Running Time. It remains to analyze the running time. The running time of step 2 can be bounded by $\widetilde{O}(|A|+|B|+|C|+mP)$ . The remaining steps 3, 4 and 5 can easily be implemented in time $\widetilde{O}(|A|+|B|+|C|+m)$ . Taking the $\log N$ iterations into account, and bounding

$$ m\leq O((P\log_{P}N)\log(P\log_{P}N))^{R}\leq(\epsilon^{-1}|A|\log N+|C|)^{1+O(\frac{\log\log N}{\log P})}, $$

the total running time can be bounded by

$$ O(P\cdot(\epsilon^{-1}|A|\log N+|B|+|C|)^{1+O(\frac{\log\log N}{\log P})})=O((\epsilon^{-1}|A|+|B|+|C|)\cdot N^{o(1)}) $$

by choosing, say, $P=2^{\sqrt{\log N}}$ (here we assumed that $|A|,|B|,|C|,\epsilon^{-1}\leq N$ ; if this is not the case, then we could simply use FFT to exactly compute $1_{A}\star 1_{B}$ in $O(N\log N)$ time, which is within the desired time bound). ∎

#### Proof of Theorem 1.9.

We design a recursive algorithm. In the base case, when $N$ is smaller than some constant threshold we can trivially solve the problem in constant time. For the recursive case, let $r$ be a parameter to be determined later and let $N^{\prime}=N/r$ (assuming for simplicity that $r$ divides $N$ ). Consider the multisets $A^{\prime}=(A\bmod N^{\prime})=\{a\bmod N^{\prime}:a\in A\}$ and $B^{\prime}=(B\bmod N^{\prime})$ (in particular, we have that $|A^{\prime}|=|A|$ and $|B^{\prime}|=|B|$ ). We compute recursively, with error parameter $\epsilon^{\prime}=\frac{\epsilon}{16}$ , a length- $2N^{\prime}$ vector $f^{\prime}$ that approximates $1_{A^{\prime}}\star 1_{B^{\prime}}$ . Then in order to compute the desired vector $f$ we proceed as follows; here we write $\operatorname{thresh}_{\alpha}(x)$ for the function that is $x$ for all $x\geq\alpha$ and zero everywhere else.

- 1. Initialize $f(c):=0$ for all $c\in[2N]$

- 2. Initialize $X:=X_{0}:=\{x\in[N^{\prime}]:f^{\prime}(x)+f^{\prime}(x+N^{\prime})>0\}$

- 3. While $X\neq\emptyset$ : 3.1. Apply Lemma 3.2 on $A,B,C:=X+\{0,N^{\prime},\dots,(2r-1)N^{\prime}\}$ and with parameter $\frac{\epsilon}{32r}$ to compute a function $g$ 3.2. For each $x\in X$ satisfying that $|f^{\prime}(x)+f^{\prime}(x+N^{\prime})-\sum_{i\in[2r]}g(x+iN^{\prime})|\leq\frac{\epsilon}{4}\cdot|B|$ : 3.2.1. Set $f(x+iN^{\prime}):=\operatorname{thresh}_{\frac{\epsilon}{2}\cdot|B|}(g(x+iN^{\prime}))$ for all $i\in[2r]$ 3.2.2. Remove $x$ from $X$

Correctness of $\lVert f-(1_{A}\star 1_{B})\rVert_{\infty}\leq\epsilon|B|$ . The proof is by induction. The base case is clearly correct, so focus on the inductive case. To prove that indeed $|f(c)-(1_{A}\star 1_{B})[c]|\leq\epsilon\cdot|B|$ we distinguish two cases. First, suppose that $c\not\in X_{0}+[2r]$ in which case the algorithm assigns $f(c)=0$ . The induction hypothesis implies that $(1_{A^{\prime}}\star 1_{B^{\prime}})[x],(1_{A^{\prime}}\star 1_{B^{\prime}})[x+N^{\prime}]\leq\frac{\epsilon}{16}\cdot|B|$ for $x=c\bmod N^{\prime}$ . It immediately follows that $(1_{A}\star 1_{B})[c]\leq\frac{\epsilon}{8}\cdot|B|$ , and thus the choice $f(c)=0$ is valid.

Next, assume that $c=x+iN^{\prime}$ for some $x\in X_{0}$ and $i\in[2r]$ . We set $f(c):=\operatorname{thresh}_{\frac{\epsilon}{2}\cdot|B|}(g(c))$ in an iteration when $|f^{\prime}(x)+f^{\prime}(x+N^{\prime})-\sum_{i\in[2r]}g(x+iN^{\prime})|\leq\frac{\epsilon}{2}\cdot|B|$ . So suppose for contradiction that $|f(c)-(1_{A}\star 1_{B})[c]|>\epsilon\cdot|B|$ and thus $|g(c)-(1_{A}\star 1_{B})[c]|>\frac{\epsilon}{2}\cdot|B|$ . As Lemma 3.2 guarantees that $g(c)\geq(1_{A}\star 1_{B})[c]$ for all $c$ , we have

$$ \displaystyle\sum_{i\in[2r]}g(x+iN^{\prime}) \displaystyle>\sum_{i\in[2r]}(1_{A}\star 1_{B})[x+iN^{\prime}]+\tfrac{\epsilon}{2}\cdot|B| \displaystyle=(1_{A^{\prime}}\star 1_{B^{\prime}})[x]+(1_{A^{\prime}}\star 1_{B^{\prime}})[x+N^{\prime}]+\tfrac{\epsilon}{2}\cdot|B| \displaystyle\geq\lparen f^{\prime}(x)-\tfrac{\epsilon}{16}\cdot|B|\rparen+\lparen f^{\prime}(x+N^{\prime})-\tfrac{\epsilon}{16}\cdot|B|\rparen+\tfrac{\epsilon}{2}\cdot|B| \displaystyle\geq f^{\prime}(x)+f^{\prime}(x+N^{\prime})+\tfrac{\epsilon}{4}\cdot|B|, $$

leading to a contradiction.

Number of Iterations. Before we continue with the remaining correctness proof, let us first bound the number of (outer) iterations of the above algorithm by $\log N$ . To this end, we show that in every iteration at least half of the elements $x\in X$ are removed. Focusing on any iteration, let us call an element $x\in X$ bad if

$$ \sum_{i\in[2r]}g(x+iN^{\prime})>\sum_{i\in[2r]}(1_{A}\star 1_{B})[x+iN^{\prime}]+\frac{\epsilon}{8}\cdot|B|, $$

and good otherwise. Given that Lemma 3.2 (applied with parameter $\frac{\epsilon}{32r}$ ) guarantees

$$ \sum_{c\in[2N]}|g(c)-(1_{A}\star 1_{B})[c]|\leq\frac{\epsilon}{32r}\cdot|B|\,|C|=\frac{\epsilon}{16}\cdot|B|\,|X|, $$

there can be at most $(\frac{\epsilon}{16}\cdot|B|\,|X|)/(\frac{\epsilon}{8}\cdot|B|)\leq\frac{1}{2}\cdot|X|$ bad elements. Moreover, for any good element $x$ we have that

$$ \left\lvert f^{\prime}(x)+f^{\prime}(x+N^{\prime})-\sum_{i\in[2r]}g(x+iN^{\prime})\right\rvert\\
\leq\left\lvert(1_{A^{\prime}}\star 1_{B^{\prime}})[x]+(1_{A^{\prime}}\star 1_{B^{\prime}})[x+N^{\prime}]-\sum_{i\in[2r]}(1_{A}\star 1_{B})[x+iN^{\prime}]\right\rvert+\frac{\epsilon}{16}+\frac{\epsilon}{16}+\frac{\epsilon}{8}, $$

and thus $x$ is indeed removed in the current iteration.

Correctness of $\lVert f\rVert_{0}\leq O(\epsilon^{-1}|A|\log^{2}N)$ . To prove the sparsity bound on $f$ , observe that in any iteration we add total mass at most

$$ \sum_{c\in[2N]}g(c)\leq O(|A|\,|B|\log N), $$

where the bound is due to Lemma 3.2. Therefore, across all $\log N$ iterations we add mass at most $\sum_{c\in[2N]}f(c)\leq O(|A|\,|B|\log^{2}N)$ . However, recall that every nonzero entry in $f$ is at least $\frac{\epsilon}{2}\cdot|B|$ due to the thresholding; the bound on the sparsity of $f$ follows.

Running Time. We finally analyze the running time of this algorithm. Ignore the cost of recursive calls for now and focus only on the above algorithm. As we showed before it runs in $\log N$ iterations, each of which is dominated by the call to Lemma 3.2 in time

$$ \displaystyle\widetilde{O}((r\epsilon^{-1}|A|+|B|+|C|)\cdot N^{o(1)}) \displaystyle=\widetilde{O}((r\epsilon^{-1}|A|+|B|+r|X|)\cdot N^{o(1)}) \displaystyle=\widetilde{O}((r\epsilon^{-1}|A|+|B|)\cdot N^{o(1)}), $$

using that $|X|\leq O(|A|/\epsilon\log^{2}N)$ as established in the previous paragraph. The remaining steps also run in time $O(r|X|)$ and can thus be similarly bounded. To take the recursion into account, let $T(N,\epsilon)$ denote the running time of this algorithm (observing that the sizes of $A$ and $B$ do not chance in recursive calls). Then:

$$ \displaystyle T(N,\epsilon) \displaystyle\leq T(\tfrac{N}{r},\tfrac{\epsilon}{16})+\widetilde{O}((r\epsilon^{-1}|A|+|B|)\cdot N^{o(1)}), \displaystyle T(N,\epsilon) \displaystyle\leq\widetilde{O}(\log_{r}(N)\cdot r\cdot 16^{\log_{r}(N)}\cdot(\epsilon^{-1}|A|+|B|)\cdot N^{o(1)}) \displaystyle\leq O((\epsilon^{-1}|A|+|B|)\cdot N^{o(1)}) $$

by setting $r=2^{\sqrt{\log N}}$ . ∎

An application of Theorem 1.9 is approximately counting 4SUM solutions. In particular, we can efficiently approximate the additive energy of a set, which will be useful later for the derandomized algorithmic BSG theorem.

#### Lemma 3.3 (Deterministic approximate 4SUM counting).

Given multisets $A,B,C,D\subseteq[N]$ of size at most $N$ , we can deterministically approximate $|\{(a,b,c,d)\in A\times B\times C\times D:a+b=c+d\}|$ up to additive error $\epsilon(|A|+|C|)|B||D|$ in $O\big(\big(\epsilon^{-1}(|A|+|C|)+|B|+|D|\big)\cdot N^{o(1)}\big)$ time.

#### Corollary 3.4.

Given a set $A\subseteq[N]$ , we can deterministically approximate its additive energy $\mathsf{E}(A)$ up to additive error $\epsilon|A|^{3}$ in $O(\epsilon^{-1}|A|N^{o(1)})$ time.

#### Proof of Lemma 3.3.

Using Theorem 1.9 we can compute an $O(\epsilon^{-1}|A|\log^{2}N)$ -sparse nonnegative vector $f$ such that $\|f-1_{A}\star 1_{B}\|_{\infty}\leq\epsilon|B|$ in $O((\epsilon^{-1}|A|+|B|)N^{o(1)})$ time, and an $O(\epsilon^{-1}|C|\log^{2}N)$ -sparse nonnegative vector $g$ such that $\|g-1_{C}\star 1_{D}\|_{\infty}\leq\epsilon|D|$ in $O((\epsilon^{-1}|C|+|D|)N^{o(1)})$ time. Then we return $\sum_{i}f[i]g[i]$ as our approximation, which has additive error

$$ \displaystyle\Big\lvert\sum_{i}(1_{A}\star 1_{B})[i](1_{C}\star 1_{D})[i]-\sum_{i}f[i]g[i]\Big\rvert \displaystyle\leq\underbrace{\Big\lvert\sum_{i}(1_{A}\star 1_{B})[i](1_{C}\star 1_{D})[i]-\sum_{i}f[i](1_{C}\star 1_{D})[i]\Big\rvert}_{=:e_{1}}+\underbrace{\Big\lvert\sum_{i}f[i](1_{C}\star 1_{D})[i]-\sum_{i}f[i]g[i]\Big\rvert}_{=:e_{2}}, $$

where

$$ \displaystyle e_{1} \displaystyle=\Big\lvert\sum_{i}\big((1_{A}\star 1_{B})[i]-f[i]\big)\cdot(1_{C}\star 1_{D})[i]\Big\rvert \displaystyle\leq\|1_{A}\star 1_{B}-f\|_{\infty}\cdot\sum_{i}(1_{C}\star 1_{D})[i] \displaystyle\leq\epsilon|B|\cdot|C||D|, $$

and

$$ \displaystyle e_{2} \displaystyle=\Big\lvert\sum_{i}f[i]\cdot\big((1_{C}\star 1_{D})[i]-g[i]\big)\Big\rvert \displaystyle\leq\|1_{C}\star 1_{D}-g\|_{\infty}\cdot\sum_{i}f[i] \displaystyle\leq\epsilon|D|\cdot\sum_{i:f[i]\neq 0}\Big(\big\lvert f[i]-(1_{A}\star 1_{B})[i]\big\rvert+(1_{A}\star 1_{B})[i]\Big) \displaystyle\leq\epsilon|D|\cdot\big(\|f\|_{0}\cdot\|f-1_{A}\star 1_{B}\|_{\infty}+\sum_{i}(1_{A}\star 1_{B})[i]\big) \displaystyle\leq\epsilon|D|\cdot\big(\epsilon^{-1}|A|\log^{2}N\cdot\epsilon|B|+|A||B|\big) \displaystyle\leq O(\epsilon|A||B||D|\log^{2}N). $$

So the total error is at most $e_{1}+e_{2}=O(\epsilon|B||D|(|A|+|C|)\log^{2}N)$ . The error can be reduced to $\epsilon|B||D|(|A|+|C|)$ after decreasing $\epsilon$ by only an $O(\log^{2}N)$ factor. The total time complexity is still $O((\epsilon^{-1}|A|+|B|)N^{o(1)})+O((\epsilon^{-1}|C|+|D|)N^{o(1)})$ as claimed. ∎

## 4 Tool II: Deterministic 3SUM Counting for Small Doubling Sets

The goal of this section is to prove the following theorem.

#### Theorem 4.1.

Given sets $A,B,C,S\subset[N]$ , we can deterministically compute

- 1. $(1_{A}\star 1_{B})[c]$ for all $c\in C$ , and

- 2. $(1_{C}\star 1_{-B})[a]$ for all $a\in A$ ,

in time complexity

$$ O\Big(\frac{|A+S|\sqrt{|B||C|}}{\sqrt{|S|}}\cdot\operatorname{\mathrm{poly}}\log(N)+\big(|A+S|+|C|\big)\cdot N^{o(1)}\Big). $$

If randomization is allowed, then the $N^{o(1)}$ factor can be replaced by $\operatorname{\mathrm{poly}}\log(N)$ .

Randomized versions of similar results were given by Abboud, Bringmann, and Fischer [ABF23], and Jin and Xu [JX23]. To deterministically implement the approaches of [ABF23, JX23], we follow the derandomization strategy of [CL15, FKP24] and work modulo some $M$ . For our purposes, we pick $M\leq|S|\cdot N^{o(1)}$ such that $S$ has many distinct remainders modulo $M$ , as stated below.

#### Lemma 4.2.

Given set $S\subseteq[N]$ , we can deterministically find an integer $M\in\big[|S|/2,|S|\cdot 2^{O(\sqrt{\log|S|\log\log N})}\big]$ in $|S|\cdot 2^{O(\sqrt{\log|S|\log\log N})}$ time such that the set $S\bmod M=\{\hat{s}\in\mathbb{Z}_{M}:\exists s\in S,s\bmod M=\hat{s}\}$ has size $|S\bmod M|\geq 0.9|S|$ .

#### Proof.

We use the same technique as [CL15]. Let $P$ be a parameter to be determined. We will iteratively pick primes $p_{1},\dots,p_{k}\in[P,2P]$ and let the final modulus be $M=p_{1}p_{2}\cdots p_{k}$ . At iteration $i$ $(i\geq 1)$ , the primes $p_{1},\dots,p_{i-1}$ are already fixed, and we pick prime $p_{i}$ to minimize

$$ h(S,p_{1}p_{2}\cdots p_{i}):=\sum_{x,y\in S,x\neq y}[x\equiv y\pmod{p_{1}p_{2}\cdots p_{i}}], $$

i.e., the number of collision pairs in $S$ modulo $p_{1}p_{2}\cdots p_{i}$ . This can be done by enumerating all primes in $[P,2P]$ , and computing $\sum_{x,y\in S}[x\equiv y\pmod{p_{1}p_{2}\cdots p_{i}}]$ in $\widetilde{O}(|S|)$ time by bucketing the elements of $S$ modulo $p_{1}p_{2}\cdots p_{i}$ and summing up the bucket sizes squared. We terminate and return $M=p_{1}\cdots p_{i}$ once the number of collision pairs $h(S,M)\leq 0.1|S|$ , in which case we must have $|S\bmod M|\geq|S|-h(S,M)\geq 0.9|S|$ and $M\geq\frac{|S|^{2}}{h(S,M)+|S|}>|S|/2$ as desired. The total time complexity is $\widetilde{O}(kP|S|)$ where $k$ is the number of iterations before termination, and $M\leq(2P)^{k}$ . We now bound $k$ .

Consider any pair of $x,y\in S,x\neq y$ where $x\equiv y\pmod{p_{1}p_{2}\cdots p_{i-1}}$ . By the prime number theorem, over a random prime $p_{i}\in[P,2P]$ , the probability that $x\equiv y\pmod{p_{1}p_{2}\cdots p_{i-1}p_{i}}$ holds is at most $O(\frac{\log_{P}N}{P/\log P})=O(\frac{\log N}{P})$ . Hence $\operatorname*{\mathbf{E}}_{p_{i}\in[P,2P]}[h(S,p_{1}\cdots p_{i})]\leq\frac{c\log N}{P}h(S,p_{1},\cdots,p_{i-1})$ by linearity of expectation (for some absolute constant $c>0$ ). By averaging, the minimizing $p_{i}\in[P,2P]$ that we choose satisfies $h(S,p_{1}\cdots p_{i})\leq\frac{c\log N}{P}h(S,p_{1}\cdots p_{i-1})$ . Since $h(S,1)=|S|(|S|-1)$ , and the second to last iteration has $h(S,p_{1}\cdots p_{k-1})>0.1|S|$ , we have

$$ k\leq 1+\frac{\log\frac{|S|(|S|-1)}{0.1|S|}}{\log\frac{P}{c\log N}}<1+\frac{\log(10|S|)}{\log\frac{P}{c\log N}}, $$

and hence

$$ M\leq(2P)^{k}<2P\cdot(10|S|)^{\log(2P)/\log(\frac{P}{c\log N})}=2P\cdot(10|S|)^{1+\frac{\log(2c\log N)}{\log(P/(c\log N))}}. $$

By choosing $P$ such that $\log P=\Theta(\sqrt{\log|S|\log\log N})$ , we have $M\leq|S|\cdot 2^{O(\sqrt{\log|S|\log\log N})}\leq|S|\cdot N^{o(1)}$ , and the time complexity is $\widetilde{O}(kP|S|)\leq|S|\cdot 2^{O(\sqrt{\log|S|\log\log N})}\leq|S|\cdot N^{o(1)}$ . ∎

The following lemma finds an efficient covering of $\mathbb{Z}_{M}$ using shifted copies of a set.

#### Lemma 4.3.

Given a set $\hat{S}\subseteq\mathbb{Z}_{M}$ , we can deterministically find a set $\Delta\subseteq\mathbb{Z}_{M}$ in $\widetilde{O}(M)$ time such that $\hat{S}+\Delta=\mathbb{Z}_{M}$ and $|\Delta|\leq(2M\ln M)/|\hat{S}|$ .

#### Proof.

Let $S_{0}=\hat{S},\Delta_{0}=\{0\}$ . Repeat the following for $i=0,1,2,\dots$ , until $S_{i}=\mathbb{Z}_{M}$ :

- • Find $\delta_{i+1}\in\mathbb{Z}_{M}$ such that $|S_{i}\cup(\delta_{i+1}+S_{i})|$ is maximized.

- • Let $S_{i+1}:=S_{i}\cup(\delta_{i+1}+S_{i})$ and $\Delta_{i+1}:=\Delta_{i}+\{0,\delta_{i+1}\}$ .

By induction, $S_{i}=\hat{S}+\Delta_{i}$ for all $i$ . When the procedure terminates with $S_{d}=\mathbb{Z}_{M}$ at iteration $i=d$ , we return $\Delta_{d}=\{0,\delta_{1}\}+\dots+\{0,\delta_{d}\}$ .

We first explain how to implement each iteration in $O(M\log M)$ time. Given $S_{i}\subseteq\mathbb{Z}_{M}$ , we use FFT to compute the cyclic convolution $f=1_{S_{i}}\star_{M}1_{-S_{i}}$ in $O(M\log M)$ time, where $f[\delta]=|(S_{i}+\delta)\cap S_{i}|$ for all $\delta\in\mathbb{Z}_{M}$ , and we pick $\delta_{i+1}=\delta$ that minimizes $f[\delta]$ and hence maximizes $|S_{i}\cup(\delta+S_{i})|=2|S_{i}|-f[\delta]$ . Then, computing $S_{i+1},\Delta_{i+1}$ takes $O(M)$ time.

Now we analyze the number of iterations $d$ . Let $\sigma_{i}=\frac{M-|S_{i}|}{M}$ be the fraction of $\mathbb{Z}_{M}$ not covered by $S_{i}$ . Observe that

$$ \operatorname*{\mathbf{E}}_{\delta\in\mathbb{Z}_{M}}\big\lvert\mathbb{Z}_{M}\setminus\big(S_{i}\cup(\delta+S_{i})\big)\big\rvert=\sum_{x\in\mathbb{Z}_{M}\setminus S_{i}}\operatorname*{\mathbf{Pr}}_{\delta\in\mathbb{Z}_{M}}[x\notin(\delta+S_{i})]=|\mathbb{Z}_{M}\setminus S_{i}|\cdot\sigma_{i}=\sigma_{i}^{2}M, $$

so $\sigma_{i+1}\leq\sigma_{i}^{2}$ by averaging. Since $S_{d-1}\neq\mathbb{Z}_{M},\sigma_{d-1}\geq\frac{1}{M}$ . Hence, the number of iterations is

$$ d\leq 1+\log_{2}\frac{\ln(1/\sigma_{d-1})}{\ln(1/\sigma_{0})}\leq\log_{2}\frac{2\ln M}{-\ln(1-|\hat{S}|/M)}\leq\log_{2}\frac{2M\ln M}{|\hat{S}|}, $$

and $|\Delta|\leq 2^{d}\leq(2M\ln M)/|\hat{S}|$ . The total time complexity is $O(dM\log M)=\widetilde{O}(M)$ . ∎

Now we prove Theorem 4.1.

#### Proof of Theorem 4.1.

Apply Lemma 4.2 to set $S$ and in $|S|\cdot 2^{O(\sqrt{\log|S|\log\log N})}=|S|\cdot N^{o(1)}$ time obtain a modulus $M\in[|S|,|S|\cdot 2^{O(\sqrt{\log|S|\log\log N})}]$ such that $\hat{S}:=S\bmod M\subseteq\mathbb{Z}_{M}$ has size $|\hat{S}|\geq|S|/2$ . Apply Lemma 4.2 to $\hat{S}$ and obtain set $\Delta\subseteq\mathbb{Z}_{M}$ in $\widetilde{O}(M)$ time such that $\hat{S}+\Delta=\mathbb{Z}_{M}$ and $|\Delta|\leq O(\frac{M\log M}{|\hat{S}|})\leq O(\frac{M\log M}{|S|})\leq 2^{O(\sqrt{\log|S|\log\log N})}$ . Compute the sumset $A+S\subset\mathbb{Z}$ in deterministic $O(|A+S|\operatorname{\mathrm{poly}}\log N)$ time via Lemma 2.1. Let $K=|A+S|/|S|$ .

#### Claim 4.4.

In $\widetilde{O}(KM+|C|)$ time, we can deterministically compute a partition of $C$ into $p=O(\log M)$ parts, $C=\bigcup_{i\in[p]}C^{(i)}$ , and shifts $\phi^{(0)},\dots,\phi^{(p-1)}\in\mathbb{Z}_{M}$ , such that for every $i\in[p]$ ,

$$ (1_{A+S}\star_{M}1_{\Delta+\phi^{(i)}})[c\bmod M]\leq O(K\log M)\text{ for all }c\in C^{(i)}. $$

#### Proof.

Compute the cyclic convolution $1_{A+S}\star_{M}1_{\Delta}$ by brute force in $O(|A+S|\cdot|\Delta|)=O(KM\log M)$ time. We have

$$ \operatorname*{\mathbf{E}}_{\hat{c}\in\mathbb{Z}_{M}}\big[(1_{A+S}\star_{M}1_{\Delta})[\hat{c}]\big]=|A+S||\Delta|/M. $$

By Markov’s inequality, the set

$$ \hat{C}_{\text{good}}:=\{\hat{c}\in\mathbb{Z}_{M}:(1_{A+S}\star_{M}1_{\Delta})[\hat{c}]\leq 2|A+S||\Delta|/M\} $$

has size $|\hat{C}_{\text{good}}|\geq M/2$ . Then, we apply Lemma 4.3 to $\hat{C}_{\text{good}}\subseteq\mathbb{Z}_{M}$ and compute in $\widetilde{O}(M)$ time a set of shifts $\Phi\subseteq\mathbb{Z}_{M}$ , $|\Phi|\leq O((M\log M)/|\hat{C}_{\text{good}}|)\leq O(\log M)$ , such that $\Phi+\hat{C}_{\text{good}}=\mathbb{Z}_{M}$ . So for every $\hat{c}\in\mathbb{Z}_{M}$ we can pick a shift $\varphi_{\hat{c}}\in\Phi$ such that $\hat{c}\in\varphi_{\hat{c}}+\hat{C}_{\text{good}}$ . Now we define a partition $C=\bigcup_{\phi\in\Phi}C_{\phi}$ where $C_{\phi}:=\{c\in C:\varphi_{c\bmod M}=\phi\}$ . Then, for all $c\in C_{\phi}$ , we have $(c\bmod M)-\phi\in\hat{C}_{\text{good}}$ , and hence

$$ (1_{A+S}\star_{M}1_{\Delta+\phi})[c\bmod M]=(1_{A+S}\star_{M}1_{\Delta})[(c\bmod M)-\phi]\leq 2|A+S||\Delta|/M\leq O(K\log M). $$

Therefore, we can return $\{(C_{\phi},\phi)\}_{\phi\in\Phi}$ as the desired $\{(C^{(i)},\phi^{(i)})\}_{i\in[p]}$ , where $p=|\Phi|=O(\log M)$ . ∎

Let $\{(C^{(i)},\phi^{(i)})\}_{i\in[p]}$ (where $p=O(\log M)$ ) be returned by Claim 4.4. In the following, we will solve the #3SUM instance $(A,B,C^{(i)})$ separately for each $i\in[p]$ , i.e., we compute the desired answers defined in the statement of Theorem 4.1 but with $C^{(i)}$ replacing $C$ . Since $C$ is the disjoint union of all $C^{(i)}$ , in the end we can easily merge these answers over all $i\in[p]$ to get the answers for the original #3SUM instance $(A,B,C)$ . This affects the total time complexity by at most a factor of $p=O(\log M)$ . From now on we focus on a particular pair of $C^{(i)}\subset\mathbb{Z}$ and $\phi^{(i)}\in\mathbb{Z}_{M}$ .

Note that

$$ (S+\Delta+\phi^{(i)})\bmod M=\hat{S}+\Delta+\phi^{(i)}=\mathbb{Z}_{M}+\phi^{(i)}=\mathbb{Z}_{M}. $$

Hence, for every $b\in\mathbb{Z}$ , there exists $s_{b}\in S$ such that $(b-s_{b})\bmod M\in\Delta+\phi^{(i)}$ . We pick such an $s_{b}$ for every $b\in B$ , in total time $\widetilde{O}(|S||\Delta+\phi^{(i)}|+|B|)=\widetilde{O}(M+|B|)$ time. Denote $d_{b}:=b-s_{b}$ , which satisfies

$$ d_{b}\bmod M\in\Delta+\phi^{(i)}. $$

Note that any 3SUM solution $(a,b,c)\in A\times B\times C^{(i)}$ where $a+b=c$ must satisfy $d_{b}=(c-a)-s_{b}\in c-(A+S)$ . This motivates the definition of the set

$$ D_{c}:=\{d\in c-(A+S):d\bmod M\in\Delta+\phi^{(i)}\} $$

for $c\in C^{(i)}$ . In this way, we can verify that the 3SUM solutions are decomposed into a disjoint union as follows (where we naturally define $B_{d}:=\{b\in B:d_{b}=d\},C_{d}:=\{c\in C^{(i)}:d\in D_{c}\}$ ),

$$ \{(a,b,c)\in A\times B\times C^{(i)}:a+b=c\}=\bigcup_{d\in\mathbb{Z}}\{(a,b,c)\in A\times B_{d}\times C_{d}:a+b=c\}. $$

Note that $B_{d}\in d+S$ by the definition of $d_{b}$ .

Before describing our final #3SUM algorithm (which relies on the decomposition in Eq. 2), we first need to give size upper bounds for the sets $C_{d}$ , and show how to compute the sets $C_{d}$ efficiently.

#### Claim 4.5.

$\sum_{d\in\mathbb{Z}}|C_{d}|=O(|C|K\log M)$ .

#### Proof.

For $c\in C^{(i)}$ , by the definition of $D_{c}$ , we have

$$ |D_{c}|=\{x\in A+S:(c-x)\bmod M\in\Delta+\phi^{(i)}\}=(1_{A+S}\star_{M}1_{\Delta+\phi^{(i)}})[c\bmod M]\underset{\text{by \lx@cref{creftype~refnum}{eqn:forallcmultbound}}}{\leq}O(K\log M). $$

Then, $\sum_{d\in\mathbb{Z}:d\bmod M\in\Delta+\phi^{(i)}}|C_{d}|=\sum_{c\in C^{(i)}}|D_{c}|\leq|C^{(i)}|\cdot O(K\log M)=O(|C|K\log M)$ . ∎

#### Claim 4.6.

We can compute all non-empty sets $C_{d}$ where $d\bmod M\in\Delta+\phi^{(i)}$ , in time $\widetilde{O}(|C||\Delta|+|A+S|)$ in addition to the output size.

#### Proof.

Equivalently, we need to compute the sets $D_{c}$ for all $c\in C^{(i)}$ . To do this, by the definition of $D_{c}$ , it suffices to list all triples in the following set,

$$ \{(\hat{d},c,x)\in(\Delta+\phi^{(i)})\times C^{(i)}\times(A+S):\hat{d}=(c-x)\bmod M\}. $$

This can be viewed as listing all solutions in an instance of 3SUM modulo $M$ . It can be done by enumerating pairs $(\hat{d},c)\in(\Delta+\phi^{(i)})\times C^{(i)}$ and searching for $x\in A+S$ , in total time $\widetilde{O}(|\Delta||C^{(i)}|+|A+S|)\leq\widetilde{O}(|\Delta||C|+|A+S|)$ in addition to the output size. ∎

Now the #3SUM algorithm for $A,B,C^{(i)}$ works as follows based on the decomposition in Eq. 2: for every $d\in\mathbb{Z}$ for which $B_{d}\neq\emptyset$ and $C_{d}\neq\emptyset$ , we solve #3SUM on $A,B_{d},C_{d}$ in one of the two ways:

- 1. Enumerate pairs in $B_{d}\times C_{d}$ and searching in $A$ , in $\widetilde{O}(|B_{d}||C_{d}|)$ time (after initially preprocessing $A$ into a binary search tree), or,

- 2. Compute $1_{A}\star 1_{B_{d}}$ using sparse convolution (Lemma 2.1) and output $(1_{A}\star 1_{B_{d}})[c]$ for all $c\in C_{d}$ , and also compute $(1_{C_{d}}\star 1_{-B_{d}})[a]$ for all $a\in A$ using Lemma 2.2, both in time complexity $O((|C_{d}|+|A+B_{d}|)\operatorname{\mathrm{poly}}\log N)=O((|C_{d}|+|A+S|)\operatorname{\mathrm{poly}}\log N)$ deterministically, where we used $B_{d}\subseteq d+S$ .

We choose Item 1 if $|B_{d}|\leq X$ for some parameter $X\geq 1$ , otherwise choose Item 2. Then, the total time over all $d\in\mathbb{Z}$ is at most (ignoring $\operatorname{\mathrm{poly}}\log(N)$ factors)

$$ \displaystyle\sum_{d\in\mathbb{Z}:|B_{d}|\leq X}|B_{d}||C_{d}|+\sum_{d\in\mathbb{Z}:|B_{d}|>X}(|C_{d}|+|A+S|) \displaystyle\leq X\cdot\sum_{d\in\mathbb{Z}}|C_{d}|+\frac{\sum_{d\in\mathbb{Z}}|B_{d}|}{X}\cdot|A+S|, $$

which can be balanced to

$$ \displaystyle O\Big(\sqrt{\sum_{d\in\mathbb{Z}}|C_{d}|\sum_{d\in\mathbb{Z}}|B_{d}|\cdot|A+S|}\Big) \displaystyle=O\Big(\sqrt{(|C|K\log M)\cdot|B|\cdot K|S|}\Big), $$

so the time complexity becomes

$$ O\Big(K\sqrt{|B||C||S|}\operatorname{\mathrm{poly}}\log(N)\Big). $$

To summarize, the total running time over all steps is (recall that $M\leq|S|\cdot N^{o(1)}$ and $|\Delta|\leq N^{o(1)}$ )

$$ \displaystyle|A+S|\operatorname{\mathrm{poly}}\log(N)+\widetilde{O}(KM+|C|)+\widetilde{O}(|C||\Delta|)+K\sqrt{|B||C||S|}\operatorname{\mathrm{poly}}\log(N) \displaystyle\leq(|A+S|+|C|)\cdot N^{o(1)}+K\sqrt{|B||C||S|}\operatorname{\mathrm{poly}}\log(N), $$

as claimed. ∎

## 5 Tool III: Almost Additive Hashing with Short Seed Length

In this section we design a small almost linear hash family $\mathcal{H}\subset\{h\colon\{-N,\dots,N\}\to\mathbb{F}_{p}\}$ that satisfies certain independence properties. Such hash family (with large size) was used in the randomized 3SUM reductions of [ABF23] and [JX23]. For our deterministic applications, we need to construct a hash family of small size, so that we can afford to enumerate all functions in the family.

Our construction is inspired by [ABF23] and [JX23], and additionally use the $\epsilon$ -biased sets of [AGHP92] to reduce the size of the family. After introducing this key ingredient in Section 5.1, we present the definitions and properties of our hash family $\mathcal{H}$ in Section 5.2. This hash family $\mathcal{H}$ will be later used in Section 6.1, Section 9.2, and Section 10.

### 5.1 Almost $k$ -wise independent distribution over $\mathbb{F}_{p}^{m}$

As a key ingredient, we will use the almost $k$ -wise independent distribution with small sample space constructed by [AGHP92]. For our purposes, we need to generalize the binary case of [AGHP92] to the mod- $p$ case, following [BS00]. The prime $p$ will be chosen small enough to fit in a machine word, so that addition and multiplication over $\mathbb{F}_{p}$ take constant time.

For vectors $a,b\in\mathbb{F}_{p}^{m}$ , let $\langle a,b\rangle\in\mathbb{F}_{p}$ denote their inner product $\sum_{i=1}^{m}a_{i}b_{i}$ .

We say a distribution over $\mathbb{F}_{p}^{k^{\prime}}$ is $\delta$ -almost uniform if it is at most $\delta$ away from the uniform distribution over $\mathbb{F}_{p}^{k^{\prime}}$ in $L_{1}$ distance. Let $\mu$ be a distribution over $\mathbb{F}_{p}^{m}$ . We say $\mu$ is $\delta$ -almost $k$ -wise independent, if for every coordinate subset $S\subseteq[m]$ of size $|S|=k^{\prime}\leq k$ , the marginal distribution of $\mu$ projected to the coordinates in $S$ is $\delta$ -almost uniform.

The following lemma summarizes the construction borrowed from [AGHP92, BS00], which will be used in the next section.

#### Lemma 5.1.

We can deterministically construct $\mathcal{C}\subset\mathbb{F}_{p}^{m}$ of size $|\mathcal{C}|\leq 4m^{2}p^{3k}$ in $\widetilde{O}(m^{3}p^{3k})$ time such that the following holds: Suppose we sample $c\in\mathcal{C}$ uniformly at random.

- 1. For any $k^{\prime}\leq k$ linearly independent vectors $x_{1},x_{2},\dots,x_{k^{\prime}}\in\mathbb{F}_{p}^{m}$ , the distribution of the $k^{\prime}$ -tuple $(\langle c,x_{1}\rangle),\dots,\langle c,x_{k^{\prime}}\rangle)\in\mathbb{F}_{p}^{k^{\prime}}$ is $\frac{1}{2p^{k-1}}$ -almost uniform.

- 2. For any $k^{\prime}<k$ vectors $x_{1},x_{2},\dots,x_{k^{\prime}}\in\mathbb{F}_{p}^{m}$ , $\operatorname*{\mathbf{Pr}}[\langle c,x_{1}\rangle=\dots=\langle c,x_{k^{\prime}}\rangle=0]\geq\frac{1}{2p^{k^{\prime}}}$ .

In the following we explain how Lemma 5.1 follows from known results in [AGHP92, BS00].

For $\gamma\in\mathbb{F}_{p}^{m}$ , define the Fourier coefficient $\mu(\gamma)=\sum_{x\in\mathbb{F}_{p}^{m}}\mu(x)\omega_{p}^{-\langle\gamma,x\rangle}$ , where $\omega_{p}=e^{2\pi i/p}$ . We say a distribution $\mu$ over $\mathbb{F}_{p}^{m}$ is $\epsilon$ -biased if $|\mu(\gamma)|\leq\epsilon$ for all $\gamma\in\mathbb{F}_{p}^{m}\setminus\{\mathbf{0}\}$ .

#### Lemma 5.2 (e.g., [AGHP92, Corollary 1]).

Every $\epsilon$ -biased distribution over $\mathbb{F}_{p}^{m}$ is $p^{k/2}\epsilon$ -almost $k$ -wise independent.

The following construction of $\epsilon$ -biased distribution is a straightforward generalization of the powering construction from [AGHP92].

#### Lemma 5.3 ([AGHP92, Section 5]).

Let $\mathbb{F}_{q}=\mathbb{F}_{p^{r}}$ be a finite field represented by a monic irreducible degree- $r$ polynomial over $\mathbb{F}_{p}$ . For $a,b\in\mathbb{F}_{q}$ , define their inner product $\langle a,b\rangle\in\mathbb{F}_{p}$ by viewing $a,b$ as vectors in $\mathbb{F}_{p}^{r}$ .

When $(x,y)$ is uniformly drawn from $\mathbb{F}_{q}\times\mathbb{F}_{q}$ , the distribution of $(\langle 1,y\rangle,\langle x,y\rangle,\dots,\langle x^{m-1},y\rangle)\in\mathbb{F}_{p}^{m}$ is $\frac{m-1}{q}$ -biased.

#### Lemma 5.4.

For an $\epsilon$ -biased distribution $\mu$ over $\mathbb{F}_{p}^{m}$ , and an invertible matrix $M\in\mathbb{F}_{p}^{m\times m}$ , the distribution of $Mx\in\mathbb{F}_{p}^{m}$ where $x\sim\mu$ is also $\epsilon$ -biased.

#### Proof.

The new distribution $M\mu$ has Fourier coefficients $\widehat{M\mu}(\gamma)=\mu(M^{\top}\gamma)$ (where $\gamma\neq\mathbf{0}$ ), which have magnitude at most $\epsilon$ since $\mu$ is $\epsilon$ -biased. ∎

Lemma 5.1 follows from putting the three lemmas together.

#### Proof of Lemma 5.1.

We prove Item 1 first. Let $\delta=\frac{1}{2p^{k-1}}$ , and $\epsilon=\delta/p^{k/2}=\frac{1}{2p^{3k/2-1}}$ . Let $r:=\lceil\log_{p}\frac{m}{\epsilon}\rceil\leq\log_{p}(2m)+3k/2$ , and $q:=p^{r}\geq m/\epsilon$ . Construct the $\frac{m-1}{q}$ -biased (and hence $\epsilon$ -biased) set $\mathcal{C}\subset\mathbb{F}_{p}^{m}$ from Lemma 5.3, which has size $|\mathcal{C}|=q^{2}=p^{2r}\leq 4m^{2}p^{3k}$ , and can be computed in $|\mathcal{C}|\cdot m\cdot\widetilde{O}(r)=\widetilde{O}(m^{3}p^{3k})$ time (constructing the finite field $\mathbb{F}_{p^{r}}$ takes $\widetilde{O}(r^{4}p^{1/2})$ time deterministically [Sho88], which is not a bottleneck). Now we verify that $\mathcal{C}$ satisfies the claimed property. Fixing $k^{\prime}\leq k$ linearly independent $x_{1},\dots,x_{k^{\prime}}\in\mathbb{F}_{p}^{m}$ , there is an invertible $m\times m$ matrix $M$ such that the first $k^{\prime}$ coordinates of $Mc$ for any $c\in\mathbb{F}_{p}^{m}$ are $\langle c,x_{1}\rangle,\dots,\langle c,x_{k^{\prime}}\rangle$ . By Lemma 5.4, the distribution of $Mc$ where $c$ is uniformly drawn from $\mathcal{C}$ is also $\epsilon$ -biased, and hence $\delta$ -almost $k$ -wise independent by Lemma 5.2. In particular, the first $k^{\prime}$ coordinates of $Mc$ , $\langle c,x_{1}\rangle,\dots,\langle c,x_{k^{\prime}}\rangle$ , are $\delta$ -almost uniform. This concludes the proof of Item 1.

Now we derive Item 2 from Item 1. Pick any maximal linear independent subset of $x_{1},\dots,x_{k^{\prime}}$ , and without loss of generality assume it contains $x_{1},\dots,x_{r}$ . Since each $x_{j}$ is a linear combination of $x_{1},\dots,x_{r}$ , we have

$$ \operatorname*{\mathbf{Pr}}[\langle c,x_{1}\rangle=\cdots=\langle c,x_{k^{\prime}}\rangle=0]=\operatorname*{\mathbf{Pr}}[\langle c,x_{1}\rangle=\cdots=\langle c,x_{r}\rangle=0]\underset{\text{by \lx@cref{creftype~refnum}{item:dethashalmostuniform}}}{\geq}\tfrac{1}{p^{r}}-\delta\geq\tfrac{1}{p^{k^{\prime}}}-\tfrac{1}{2p^{k-1}}\geq\tfrac{1}{2p^{k^{\prime}}} $$

as claimed. ∎

### 5.2 Almost linear hashing with “almost” almost $k$ -wise independence

Let $k\geq 2$ be a fixed constant integer. We now construct our hash family $\mathcal{H}\subset\{h\colon\{-N,\dots,N\}\to\mathbb{F}_{p}\}$ . In the following we assume the universe size $N$ is larger than some big constant (possibly dependent on $k$ ) in order to simplify some calculation.

#### Definition 5.5 (Hash family $\mathcal{H}$ ).

Let $k\geq 2$ be a fixed constant integer. Given universe size $N$ and a prime parameter $p\geq\log^{2k}N$ , define a hash family $\mathcal{H}\subset\{h\colon\{-N,\dots,N\}\to\mathbb{F}_{p}\}$ as follows:

- • Let

$$ Q:=100\log N<p. $$

Deterministically pick distinct primes $q_{1},q_{2},\dots,q_{m-1}\in[Q/2,Q]$ such that

$$ q_{1}q_{2}\cdots q_{m-1}\in[N(\log N)^{2k},N(\log N)^{3k}], $$

(3) which is possible since the product of all primes in the interval $[50\log N,100\log N]$ is at least $N^{2}$ (by the Prime Number Theorem, e.g. [RS62]). In particular,

$$ m=(1+o(1))\tfrac{\log N}{\log\log N}. $$

- • Draw a random $c\in\mathbb{F}_{p}^{m}$ from Lemma 5.1 with parameters $p,m,k$ . Then, for $x\in\{-N,\dots,N\}$ , define vector $w=(x\bmod q_{1},x\bmod q_{2},\dots,x\bmod q_{m-1},1)\in\mathbb{F}_{p}^{m}$ (where each $x\bmod q_{i}$ is converted into $\{0,1,\dots,q_{i}-1\}\subset\mathbb{F}_{p}$ ), and let the hash value of $x$ be $h(x):=\langle c,w\rangle$ .

By Lemma 5.1, this hash family has size $|\mathcal{H}|\leq 4m^{2}p^{3k}$ and can be computed in $\widetilde{O}(m^{3}p^{3k})$ time (the time for computing $q_{1},\dots,q_{m-1}$ is $O(logN)=o(p)$ and is negligible), and each hash function $h\in\mathcal{H}$ can be evaluated at any given $x$ in $O(m)=o(\log N)$ time.

First, we show that the hash family $\mathcal{H}$ is almost linear.

#### Lemma 5.6 (Almost linearity, $\Delta_{h}$ ).

In Definition 5.5, for every $h\in\mathcal{H}$ (defined using $c\in\mathbb{F}_{p}^{m}$ ), we have $h(x+y)-h(x)-h(y)\in\Delta_{h}$ for all $x,y\in\{-N,\dots,N\}$ , where $\Delta_{h}\subseteq\mathbb{F}_{p}$ is defined as the iterative sumset,

$$ \Delta_{h}:=\{0,-q_{1}c_{1}\}+\{0,-q_{2}c_{2}\}+\dots+\{0,-q_{m-1}c_{m-1}\}+c_{m} $$

with size $|\Delta_{h}|\leq 2^{m-1}=N^{o(1)}$ .

#### Proof.

Note that $q_{i}\leq Q<p$ for all $i$ . For any $x,y\in\mathbb{Z}$ ,

$$ h(x+y)-h(x)-h(y)=c_{m}+\sum_{i=1}^{m-1}c_{i}\cdot\big(((x+y)\bmod q_{i})-(x\bmod q_{i})-(y\bmod q_{i})\big). $$

By $((x+y)\bmod q_{i})-(x\bmod q_{i})-(y\bmod q_{i})\in\{0,-q_{i}\}$ , the claim immediately follows. ∎

Using almost linearity, we now show that the hash values of Sidon 4-tuples under $\mathcal{H}$ are highly correlated. Recall that for a set $\Delta$ , we define the iterative sumset $k\Delta=(k-1)\Delta+\Delta$ .

#### Lemma 5.7 (Hashing Sidon 4-tuples).

Suppose integers $x,y,z,w\in[N]$ satisfy $x+y=z+w$ . Then the hash family $\mathcal{H}$ from Definition 5.5 (with $k\geq 3$ ) satisfies

$$ \operatorname*{\mathbf{Pr}}_{h\in\mathcal{H}}\big[\exists i\in\mathbb{F}_{p}:\{h(x),h(y),h(z),h(w)\}\subseteq i+\Delta^{\prime}_{h}\big]\geq\frac{1}{2p^{2}}, $$

where $\Delta^{\prime}_{h}:=3(\{0\}\cup\Delta_{h})\subseteq\mathbb{F}_{p}$ , with size $|\Delta^{\prime}_{h}|<(|\Delta_{h}|+1)^{3}\leq 2^{3m}=N^{o(1)}$ .

#### Proof.

By the definition of $h$ and by Item 2 of Lemma 5.1, we have $h(x-y)=h(y-z)=0$ with at least $\frac{1}{2p^{2}}$ probability. Since $y-z=w-x$ , in this case we also have $h(w-x)=0$ . Then, by Lemma 5.6, we have $h(y)-h(z)\in\Delta_{h},h(x)-h(y)\in\Delta_{h}$ , and $h(w)-h(x)\in\Delta_{h}$ . So $h(y)\in h(z)+\Delta_{h},h(x)\in h(z)+\Delta_{h}+\Delta_{h}$ , and $h(w)\in h(z)+\Delta_{h}+\Delta_{h}+\Delta_{h}$ . Then, for $i=h(z)$ , we have $\{h(x),h(y),h(z),h(w)\}\subseteq\{i\}\cup\{i+\Delta_{h}\}\cup\{i+2\Delta_{h}\}\cup\{i+3\Delta_{h}\}=i+\Delta^{\prime}_{h}$ . ∎

To state the next property of $\mathcal{H}$ , we need the following definition (which also appeared in [JX23]):
